Spring Boot: setup, configuration and diagnostics

## Project setup

A Boot project inherits dependency versions from the Spring Boot BOM (through the `spring-boot-starter-parent` Maven parent or the Gradle plugin with dependency management). Starters such as `spring-boot-starter-web`, `-data-jpa`, `-security`, `-test` and `-actuator` bring in a consistent set of libraries; leave their versions to the BOM unless you have a reason. Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17 or later and uses `jakarta.*` packages instead of `javax.*`; mixing libraries built for `javax` causes `ClassNotFoundException` or missing beans.

`./mvnw spring-boot:run` or `./gradlew bootRun` run the app; the build produces an executable jar.

## Externalized configuration

Properties come from many sources with a defined precedence. From lower to higher (selected): defaults in `application.properties`/`application.yml` inside the jar, profile-specific files (`application-dev.yml`), files outside the jar, OS environment variables, Java system properties, and command-line arguments. Higher sources override lower ones. Environment variables use relaxed binding: `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` sets `spring.datasource.url`.

Keep secrets out of committed files; supply them through environment variables or a secret store.

## Binding configuration to types

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "mentor.retrieval")
public record RetrievalProperties(int topK, Duration timeout) {}
```

Enable it with `@EnableConfigurationProperties(RetrievalProperties.class)` or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`. Records and constructor binding give immutable settings. Add `@Validated` and Bean Validation annotations to fail at startup on bad values. `@Value("${...}")` reads single values but gives no type-safe grouping or validation.

## Profiles

`spring.profiles.active=dev` activates profile-specific files and `@Profile("dev")` beans. Profiles are for environment differences (local database, logging), not feature flags. In Boot 2.4+ `spring.profiles.active` cannot be set inside a profile-specific document.

## Auto-configuration

Boot's auto-configuration classes create beans when conditions hold: a class is on the classpath (`@ConditionalOnClass`), a property is set, or no user-defined bean of that type exists (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`). Defining your own bean of a type usually makes the auto-configured one back off. Run with `--debug` (or `debug=true`) to print the conditions evaluation report, which explains why each auto-configuration did or did not apply. Exclude one with `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = ...)` or `spring.autoconfigure.exclude`.

## Operational diagnostics with Actuator

`spring-boot-starter-actuator` adds endpoints such as `/actuator/health`, `/actuator/info`, `/actuator/metrics`, `/actuator/env`, `/actuator/beans`, `/actuator/conditions` and `/actuator/loggers`. Over HTTP, only `health` is exposed by default; expose others with `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. Endpoints such as `env`, `beans` and `heapdump` reveal sensitive details, so protect them and avoid exposing them publicly.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which property source supplied the value your application actually used?
- What does the conditions report say about the auto-configuration you expected?
- Which profile was active when this bean was created?

Spring Core: dependency injection and beans

## The container

The Spring `ApplicationContext` creates objects called beans, wires their dependencies and manages their lifecycle. You describe beans; the container decides when to construct them and what to inject.

## Defining beans

- Component scanning: classes annotated with `@Component` or a specialization (`@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`, `@RestController`) in scanned packages become beans. In Spring Boot, scanning starts at the package of the `@SpringBootApplication` class, so classes outside that package tree are not found unless configured.
- `@Configuration` classes with `@Bean` methods define beans explicitly, which suits third-party classes you cannot annotate. In full `@Configuration` mode, calls between `@Bean` methods return the container's singleton rather than a new object, because the class is proxied by CGLIB.

## Injection

Constructor injection is the recommended default: dependencies are explicit, can be `final`, and the class is easy to construct in a unit test. With a single constructor, `@Autowired` is optional. Field injection hides dependencies and needs reflection or the container in tests.

When several beans match a type, injection fails with `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. Resolve with `@Primary`, `@Qualifier("name")`, or by injecting `List<Type>` or `Map<String, Type>` to receive all of them. A missing dependency fails startup with `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`; `Optional<T>` or `ObjectProvider<T>` express optional dependencies.

Circular constructor dependencies fail at startup. Spring Boot 2.6 and later prohibit circular references by default. Restructure the dependency rather than switching to field injection to hide it.

## Scopes

- `singleton` (default): one instance per container. It must be safe for concurrent use in web applications, so avoid mutable per-request fields.
- `prototype`: a new instance each time it is requested from the container. Injecting a prototype into a singleton happens once, so the singleton keeps one instance; use `ObjectProvider<T>` to get fresh ones.
- Web scopes: `request`, `session`, `application` (and `websocket`). Injecting them into singletons requires a scoped proxy.

## Lifecycle

Construction, dependency injection, then initialization callbacks (`@PostConstruct`, `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet`, or `@Bean(initMethod=...)`), then use, then destruction callbacks on context shutdown (`@PreDestroy`). The container does not call destruction callbacks for prototype beans. `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` come from `jakarta.annotation` in Spring 6.

## Proxies and self-invocation

Features such as `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable` and method security are implemented by wrapping the bean in a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy for interfaces, or CGLIB subclass). Only calls that go through the proxy are intercepted. Consequences:

- Calling an annotated method from another method of the same class (`this.save()`) bypasses the proxy, so the annotation has no effect.
- With CGLIB proxies, `final` methods and `private` methods cannot be intercepted.
- The bean you receive is the proxy, not your class instance; `getClass()` shows a generated subclass.

## Diagnostics

Startup failures print the bean creation chain ("Error creating bean with name ... Unsatisfied dependency expressed through constructor parameter 0"). Read from the innermost cause outwards. In Spring Boot, the `FailureAnalyzer` summary at the end usually names the missing or ambiguous bean.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Is the class you expect to be injected inside the package tree that is being scanned?
- Does this call go through the Spring proxy, or is it a call on `this`?
- How many instances of this prototype bean does the singleton actually see?

Spring Data JPA: relationships, transactions and query behaviour

## Entities and relationships

- `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` are lazy by default; `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` are eager by default in JPA. Making to-one associations `fetch = FetchType.LAZY` is common practice, so data is loaded only when used.
- In a bidirectional relationship, one side owns it (`@ManyToOne` side, or the side without `mappedBy`). Only changes to the owning side are written. Keep both sides in sync in helper methods.
- `equals`/`hashCode` on entities based on generated IDs break when the ID is still null before persisting; base them on a business key or follow the provider's guidance.

## The N+1 problem

Loading a list of N parents and then touching a lazy collection on each one issues 1 query for the list plus N queries for the collections. Detect it by logging SQL (`spring.jpa.show-sql` for quick checks, or a proper logger such as `org.hibernate.SQL`) or by counting statements in tests. Fixes: a fetch join (`select p from Problem p join fetch p.tags`), an `@EntityGraph` on the repository method, batch fetching (`hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size`), or a DTO projection that selects exactly the needed columns. Fetch joins combined with pagination on collections make Hibernate paginate in memory and log a warning; paginate the parent IDs first instead.

## Transactions

- `@Transactional` on a public method of a Spring bean starts or joins a transaction through a proxy. Self-invocation bypasses it (see the Spring Core reference).
- By default, rollback happens for unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException`, `Error`) only; checked exceptions commit unless `rollbackFor` is set.
- Repository methods from `SimpleJpaRepository` are transactional themselves (read-only for queries).
- `readOnly = true` is a hint that can skip dirty checking and lets some drivers route to replicas; it does not by itself forbid writes on every database.
- Within a transaction, managed entities are dirty-checked and changes are flushed at commit without calling `save`.
- Open Session in View (`spring.jpa.open-in-view`, true by default in Boot, with a startup warning) keeps the persistence context open during view rendering, which hides lazy-loading problems and holds connections longer. Many teams disable it.

## Locking

- Optimistic locking: a `@Version` field. Concurrent updates fail with `ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException`; the caller retries or reports a conflict.
- Pessimistic locking: `@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)` on a query issues `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on databases that support it. Holding locks long blocks other transactions and can deadlock.

## Query methods

Derived queries (`findByEmailAndActiveTrue`), `@Query` with JPQL or native SQL, and projections (interfaces or records). `existsBy...` and `countBy...` avoid loading entities. `Pageable` adds `LIMIT/OFFSET` and a count query; `Slice` skips the count when only "is there a next page" matters.

## Schema migrations

Production schemas should be managed by versioned migrations with Flyway (`db/migration/V1__init.sql`) or Liquibase, which Boot runs at startup when the dependency is present. `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update` is convenient for prototypes but does not handle renames, data migrations or rollbacks reliably; use `validate` or `none` with migrations.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- How many SQL statements does this endpoint run for a page of 20 items?
- Which exception type is thrown here, and will the transaction roll back?
- Which side of this relationship owns it, and did you change that side?

Spring MVC for REST APIs

## Request lifecycle

`DispatcherServlet` receives every request, finds a handler through the handler mappings, resolves method arguments, invokes the controller method, and converts the return value into a response with an `HttpMessageConverter` (Jackson for JSON). Servlet filters (including Spring Security's) run before the `DispatcherServlet`; `HandlerInterceptor`s run around handler execution.

## Routing and arguments

```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/problems")
class ProblemController {
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    ProblemView get(@PathVariable long id) { ... }

    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<ProblemView> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateProblem body) { ... }
}
```

- `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam` (with `required` and `defaultValue`), `@RequestHeader`, `@RequestBody`.
- Compile with `-parameters` (the Boot build plugins do this) or name parameters explicitly; Spring 6.1 no longer infers names from debug information.
- Spring 6 no longer matches a trailing slash by default: `/api/problems/` does not map to `/api/problems`.
- `ResponseEntity` sets status and headers; `@ResponseStatus` sets a fixed status.

## Request and response contracts

Use dedicated request and response types (records work well) instead of exposing JPA entities. Entities leak internal fields, can trigger lazy loading during serialization, and can cause infinite recursion on bidirectional relationships. Jackson configuration (`spring.jackson.*` properties or a `Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer`) controls date formats, unknown-property handling and naming.

## Validation

Add `spring-boot-starter-validation`. `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody` runs Bean Validation (`@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Min`, `@Email`, ...) and fails with `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (HTTP 400). Validation of `@RequestParam` and `@PathVariable` constraints needs `@Validated` on the controller in older versions; Spring 6.1 added built-in method validation for controllers.

## Errors

- `@ExceptionHandler` methods in a `@RestControllerAdvice` map exceptions to responses in one place.
- Spring 6 supports RFC 9457 problem details (`ProblemDetail`, `ErrorResponse`). Enable `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` in Boot to render built-in errors that way, or extend `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`.
- Do not return stack traces or internal messages to clients.

## Pagination

Return a page of results plus enough information for the next request. With Spring Data, a `Pageable` parameter binds `page`, `size` and `sort` query parameters. Cap `size` (`spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size`) so clients cannot request everything. Serializing `PageImpl` directly is discouraged in recent Spring Data versions because its JSON structure is not a stable contract; use `PagedModel` or your own response type. Offset pagination slows down on deep pages; keyset (cursor) pagination on an indexed column scales better.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which layer turns this exception into a response, and what does the client receive?
- What does the client see if you return the entity directly and it has a lazy collection?
- What stops a client from requesting a page size of one million?

Spring Security for servlet applications

## Architecture

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters registered through `DelegatingFilterProxy` and `FilterChainProxy`. Each `SecurityFilterChain` bean matches some requests and runs an ordered list of filters: CORS, CSRF, authentication filters (form login, HTTP Basic, bearer token), exception translation and authorization. Because filters run before Spring MVC, a request rejected by security never reaches your controller or its `@ExceptionHandler`.

```java
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}
```

Rules are evaluated in order; put specific matchers before general ones. Adding the starter without configuration secures every endpoint with a generated password printed at startup.

## Authentication

An `Authentication` object represents the principal and authorities. It is stored in the `SecurityContext` (per thread by default). `AuthenticationManager` delegates to `AuthenticationProvider`s, often backed by a `UserDetailsService` and a `PasswordEncoder`. Store passwords with an adaptive hash; `PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()` defaults to bcrypt and prefixes the algorithm id (`{bcrypt}`).

## Authorization

- Request-level rules in `authorizeHttpRequests`.
- Method security with `@EnableMethodSecurity` and `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")`, implemented by proxies (self-invocation bypasses them).
- `hasRole("ADMIN")` checks the authority `ROLE_ADMIN`; `hasAuthority("SCOPE_read")` checks the exact string. JWT scopes become `SCOPE_` authorities by default.
- Unauthenticated requests get 401 (through the `AuthenticationEntryPoint`); authenticated but forbidden ones get 403 (`AccessDeniedHandler`).

## Sessions and tokens

- Browser apps with form login typically use a server-side session cookie. Session fixation protection changes the session ID on login.
- Stateless APIs often validate bearer tokens (JWT or opaque) with the OAuth2 resource server support. Configure the issuer (`spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri`) so signatures, expiry and issuer are checked. Short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens limit the damage of a leaked token; revocation of self-contained JWTs needs extra infrastructure.
- Do not log tokens or credentials.

## CSRF

CSRF protection is on by default for state-changing methods (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE). It matters when the browser sends credentials automatically, such as session cookies. APIs authenticated only by bearer tokens in an `Authorization` header are generally not exposed to CSRF, which is why such APIs often disable it; disabling it for cookie-based sessions is a vulnerability. Single-page apps using cookies need the token exposed in a readable cookie or header (`CookieCsrfTokenRepository`), following the documented SPA configuration for the Spring Security version.

## CORS

CORS is a browser rule about which origins may read responses; it is not authentication. Configure it with `http.cors(...)` and a `CorsConfigurationSource` so preflight `OPTIONS` requests are handled before authentication. Allow specific origins; `allowCredentials(true)` cannot be combined with a wildcard origin.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which filter rejected this request, and why does your controller's exception handler never see it?
- Is this API authenticated by a cookie or by a header, and what does that mean for CSRF?
- Which authority string does `hasRole("ADMIN")` look for?

Spring testing: choosing the boundary

This reference explains testing concepts for learning Spring. It does not define assessments.

## Three layers

| Kind | What starts | Typical tools | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | No Spring context; construct the class directly | JUnit, Mockito, AssertJ | Business logic, algorithms in services |
| Slice | A partial context for one layer | `@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, `@JsonTest`, `@RestClientTest` | Controllers, repositories, serialization |
| Integration | The full application context | `@SpringBootTest`, Testcontainers | Wiring, configuration, real database behaviour |

Constructor injection makes unit tests simple: pass fakes or mocks to the constructor without Spring.

## Slices

- `@WebMvcTest(ProblemController.class)` loads MVC infrastructure, the controller, `@ControllerAdvice`, filters and security configuration, but not services or repositories. Provide collaborators as mocks. Use `MockMvc` (or `MockMvcTester` in Boot 3.4+) to send requests and check status, headers and JSON.
- `@DataJpaTest` configures JPA repositories and, by default, replaces the datasource with an embedded database and wraps each test in a transaction that rolls back. An embedded database can behave differently from the production database (SQL dialect, locking, constraints); `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` with Testcontainers tests against the real engine.

## Full context

`@SpringBootTest` starts the whole application. `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` starts a real server for HTTP-level tests with `TestRestTemplate` or `WebTestClient`. Spring caches contexts between test classes with the same configuration; each distinct combination of mocks, properties or profiles creates a new context and slows the suite. `@DirtiesContext` discards a context and should be rare.

Testcontainers with `@ServiceConnection` (Boot 3.1+) starts databases or brokers in containers and wires their connection details automatically. It needs a container runtime such as Docker on the machine running the tests.

## Mocks in the context

`@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` (Spring Framework 6.2, Boot 3.4) replace a bean in the context with a Mockito mock or spy. The older Boot `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean` are deprecated from Boot 3.4. Each different set of mocked beans is a different context cache key.

## Fixtures

Create test data in the test or in builders and factory methods, not in shared mutable state. `@Sql` runs scripts before a test. Transactional tests roll back by default, but code that runs in a new transaction (`REQUIRES_NEW`, async threads, a real HTTP call to `RANDOM_PORT`) commits and is not rolled back, so clean up explicitly.

## Security testing

With `spring-security-test`: `@WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN")` runs a test as an authenticated user; with MockMvc, request post-processors such as `.with(csrf())`, `.with(user("ana").roles("USER"))` and `.with(jwt())` add a CSRF token or a principal. Test both the allowed path and the 401 and 403 paths.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which beans does this slice actually create, and which ones must you supply?
- Does this test talk to the same database engine as production?
- Why does adding one more mocked bean make the whole test suite slower?

Django middleware, authentication and security

## Middleware

`MIDDLEWARE` is an ordered list. On the way in, middleware runs top to bottom; on the way out, bottom to top. Order matters: `SessionMiddleware` must come before `AuthenticationMiddleware`, which sets `request.user`; `SecurityMiddleware` usually comes first. A middleware is a callable that takes `get_response` and returns a callable taking `request`.

## Authentication

- `django.contrib.auth` provides users, groups, permissions, password hashing and login views. Passwords are hashed with PBKDF2 by default; Argon2 and others can be configured in `PASSWORD_HASHERS`.
- Start a new project with a custom user model (`AUTH_USER_MODEL`) even if it only subclasses `AbstractUser`. Switching later, after migrations exist, is difficult.
- Refer to the user model through `settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL` in foreign keys and `get_user_model()` in code.
- `login_required` (function views), `LoginRequiredMixin` (class-based views) and, since Django 5.1, `LoginRequiredMiddleware` with `login_not_required` for exceptions.
- `request.user.is_authenticated`; `AnonymousUser` for logged-out requests.

## Permissions

Model permissions (`add`, `change`, `delete`, `view`) are created per model. Check with `user.has_perm("app.change_problem")`, `permission_required`, or `PermissionRequiredMixin`. Built-in permissions are per model, not per object; object-level rules ("only the author may edit") must be enforced in the view or queryset (`Problem.objects.filter(author=request.user)`) or with a third-party backend. Always scope querysets by the current user where ownership matters, so an ID in the URL cannot be used to reach another user's data.

## Security features and settings

- CSRF: `CsrfViewMiddleware` checks a token on unsafe methods. `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` must list origins (with scheme) when requests come from other hosts over HTTPS.
- XSS: template auto-escaping; be careful with `|safe`.
- SQL injection: the ORM parameterizes queries; `raw()` and `extra()` with string formatting reintroduce the risk. Pass parameters separately.
- Clickjacking: `XFrameOptionsMiddleware`.
- `DEBUG = False` in production. With `DEBUG = True`, error pages expose settings and code.
- `SECRET_KEY` must be secret and must not be committed; it signs sessions, password reset tokens and more.
- `ALLOWED_HOSTS` must list served host names when `DEBUG` is false.
- HTTPS settings: `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`, `CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE`, `SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS`, and `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` when behind a proxy that terminates TLS.

`python manage.py check --deploy` reports many missing production settings.

## Configuration

Settings are a Python module selected by `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE`. Common practice reads secrets and environment-specific values from environment variables (directly or with libraries such as django-environ) and keeps one settings module per environment or a base module with overrides. Settings are read at startup; changing them at run time is not supported except in tests (`override_settings`).

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- If a logged-in user changes the ID in this URL, which rows can they reach?
- In which order do these two middleware classes see the request, and does the second depend on the first?
- What does `check --deploy` report for this settings file?

Django models, QuerySets and migrations

This is a framework reference, not DSA-in-Django context.

## Models

A model class maps to a table; fields map to columns. `ForeignKey` needs `on_delete` (`CASCADE`, `PROTECT`, `SET_NULL`, ...), which decides what happens to rows that reference a deleted row. `related_name` names the reverse accessor (`author.books`). `Meta` sets ordering, constraints (`UniqueConstraint`, `CheckConstraint`) and indexes. Database constraints protect data even when code bypasses model validation; `full_clean()` is not called by `save()` automatically.

## QuerySets are lazy

`Book.objects.filter(published=True).order_by("-created")` builds a query without running it. Evaluation happens on iteration, `len()`, `list()`, slicing with a step, `bool()`, `repr()` in the shell, and methods such as `get`, `count`, `exists`, `first`. A QuerySet caches its results after the first full evaluation; building a new QuerySet (another `.filter()`) runs a new query.

- `get()` raises `DoesNotExist` or `MultipleObjectsReturned`; `first()` returns `None` when empty.
- `exists()` and `count()` are cheaper than loading rows when you only need those answers.
- Slicing (`[:20]`) adds `LIMIT`/`OFFSET`.
- `F("views") + 1` and `update()` perform updates in the database, avoiding read-modify-write races in Python.
- `Q` objects combine conditions with `|`, `&` and `~`.
- `annotate` and `aggregate` with `Count`, `Sum`, `Avg` compute in SQL.

## N+1 queries

Accessing `book.author` for each book in a loop issues one query per book unless the relation was preloaded:

- `select_related("author")` joins forward `ForeignKey` and `OneToOne` relations in the same query.
- `prefetch_related("tags")` loads many-to-many and reverse relations with one extra query per relation and joins them in Python. `Prefetch(...)` customizes the inner query.
- `only()`/`defer()` limit columns; `values()`/`values_list()` return dicts or tuples instead of model instances.

Inspect queries with `connection.queries` (when `DEBUG=True`), `QuerySet.explain()`, Django Debug Toolbar, or `assertNumQueries` in tests.

## Transactions

By default each query autocommits. `transaction.atomic()` (decorator or context manager) groups work into one transaction and rolls back on exception; nested `atomic` blocks create savepoints. `ATOMIC_REQUESTS = True` wraps each view in a transaction. `select_for_update()` locks selected rows until the transaction ends and must run inside `atomic`. `transaction.on_commit(fn)` defers side effects such as sending email until the commit succeeds.

## Migrations

`makemigrations` writes migration files from model changes; `migrate` applies them. Migrations are code: commit them, review them, and do not edit ones already applied elsewhere. Data migrations use `RunPython` with the historical model from `apps.get_model`, not the current model class. On large tables, adding a non-null column with a default, or an index, can lock the table depending on the database; check the database's behaviour. `sqlmigrate` shows the SQL a migration will run.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- How many queries does this template trigger for a list of 50 books?
- At which line does this QuerySet actually hit the database?
- If two requests increment this counter at the same time, which update can be lost?

Django routing, views, forms and templates

## Request flow

A request passes through middleware, is matched against `urlpatterns` starting at `ROOT_URLCONF`, and the matched view returns an `HttpResponse`. Middleware then processes the response on the way out.

## URLs

```python
urlpatterns = [
    path("problems/", views.problem_list, name="problem-list"),
    path("problems/<int:pk>/", views.ProblemDetail.as_view(), name="problem-detail"),
    path("api/", include("api.urls")),
]
```

- Path converters (`int`, `slug`, `uuid`, `path`, `str`) validate and convert captured values.
- Patterns are tried in order; the first match wins.
- Name routes and build URLs with `reverse("problem-detail", args=[pk])` or `{% url %}` instead of hard-coding paths. `app_name` in an included URLconf adds a namespace.

## Views

- Function views take `request` and return a response. `get_object_or_404` turns a missing row into a 404 instead of a 500.
- Class-based views (`ListView`, `DetailView`, `CreateView`, `UpdateView`, `View`) provide common patterns; override methods such as `get_queryset` and `get_context_data`. Restrict methods with `require_POST` or `http_method_names`.
- Redirect after a successful POST (`redirect(...)`) so reloading the page does not resubmit the form.
- Django supports async views (`async def`); the ORM's async API (`aget`, `acount`, async iteration) exists, but parts of Django and many third-party apps are still synchronous and run in a thread pool under ASGI.

## Forms

A `Form` or `ModelForm` declares fields, converts submitted strings into Python values and validates them.

- Bind data with `form = ProblemForm(request.POST)`, then `form.is_valid()`. Read cleaned values from `form.cleaned_data`, never from `request.POST` directly.
- Field-specific validation goes in `clean_<field>()`, cross-field validation in `clean()`. Raise `ValidationError` with a message.
- `ModelForm.save(commit=False)` returns an unsaved instance so you can set extra fields.
- Render errors back to the user: unbound or invalid forms keep their data and errors.

## Templates

- `{{ value }}` output is HTML-escaped by default, which prevents most cross-site scripting through templates. `|safe` and `mark_safe` turn escaping off; use them only for content you have sanitized.
- `{% csrf_token %}` must appear inside every POST form rendered by Django when CSRF middleware is enabled.
- Template lookups (`{{ book.author.name }}`) can trigger queries; preload relations in the view (see the ORM reference).
- `{% extends %}` and `{% block %}` build layouts; `{% include %}` reuses fragments.

FastAPI dependencies, lifespan and resource lifetime

This is a framework reference, not DSA-in-FastAPI context.

## Depends

```python
def get_settings() -> Settings: ...

@app.get("/problems/{pid}")
async def read_problem(pid: int, settings: Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)]): ...
```

FastAPI calls dependencies for each request, injects their results, and caches each dependency's result within one request: if two parameters depend on the same function, it runs once per request unless `use_cache=False`. Dependencies can depend on other dependencies, which builds a graph. The `Annotated[T, Depends(fn)]` form is the recommended style in current documentation.

Dependencies are not singletons across requests. For process-wide objects (configuration, a connection pool, an HTTP client, a loaded model), create them once at startup and read them from `app.state`, or cache a factory with `functools.lru_cache`.

## Dependencies with yield

A dependency that `yield`s provides a value and runs cleanup after it:

```python
def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
```

The exact point at which the code after `yield` runs (before or after the response is sent, and whether it can still change the response) changed in FastAPI 0.106.0 and again in 0.118.0. From 0.106.0 the exit code ran before the response was sent, which closed database sessions too early for `StreamingResponse`; 0.118.0 moved it back to after the response is sent. From 0.121.0, `Depends(dep, scope="function")` runs the exit code as soon as the path operation returns; the default, `scope="request"`, runs it after the response is sent. Check the release notes for the installed version before relying on cleanup timing, for example when streaming responses use the session.

## Lifespan

`FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)` takes an async context manager. Code before `yield` runs at startup, code after it at shutdown. It replaces the older `@app.on_event("startup")` handlers, which are deprecated. Use it to open and close pools, clients and background resources. Lifespan runs once per worker process; with several Uvicorn or Gunicorn workers, each has its own copy.

## Database session lifetime

- One session per request, provided by a yield dependency, is the common pattern. Do not share a session object across requests or concurrent tasks; SQLAlchemy sessions are not safe for concurrent use.
- Commit explicitly where the work succeeds; on exceptions, roll back (the session's context manager or `finally` handles this when written correctly).
- With synchronous SQLAlchemy, define the path operation and the dependency with plain `def`, so FastAPI runs them in a thread pool. With `AsyncSession` and an async driver, use `async def` throughout.
- Lazy loading after the session closes raises `DetachedInstanceError`. Load what the response needs before returning, or convert to response models inside the request.

## Authentication

`fastapi.security` provides helpers (`OAuth2PasswordBearer`, `HTTPBearer`, `APIKeyHeader`) that extract credentials from requests and add them to the OpenAPI schema. They do not verify anything: a dependency such as `get_current_user` must decode and validate the token (signature, expiry, issuer, audience), look up the user, and raise `HTTPException(401)` with a `WWW-Authenticate` header on failure. Authorization (roles, ownership) is a further dependency or check. Hash passwords with a maintained library (the current tutorial uses `pwdlib` with Argon2; older versions used passlib).

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- How many times does this dependency run in one request, and across requests?
- When does the cleanup after `yield` run in the FastAPI version this project pins?
- Which line actually checks that the token is valid, as opposed to just reading it?

FastAPI validation, responses and async boundaries

## Request validation

FastAPI reads path parameters, query parameters, headers, cookies and bodies according to the function signature and validates them with Pydantic.

- A parameter in the path template is a path parameter; a simple type not in the path is a query parameter; a Pydantic model is the JSON body.
- `Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)]`, `Path(...)` and `Field(...)` add constraints.
- Invalid input produces a 422 response with a list of errors (location, message, type). This is FastAPI's default error contract; clients and tests can rely on its shape for that version.
- Pydantic v2 is strict about some conversions that v1 allowed and lax about others (strings like `"5"` still convert to `int` in lax mode). `model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)` or `Strict` types make validation strict. Unknown fields are ignored by default; `extra="forbid"` rejects them.

## Response models

`response_model=ProblemOut` (or a return type annotation) validates and filters the returned data. Use separate input and output models so internal fields, such as password hashes or owner IDs, never leak into responses. `response_model_exclude_unset` and similar options control which fields appear. Converting ORM objects requires `model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)` in Pydantic v2 (formerly `orm_mode`).

## Errors

- Raise `HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Problem not found")` for expected client errors.
- Register handlers with `@app.exception_handler(MyError)` to map domain exceptions to responses in one place, and override `RequestValidationError` handling only if clients need a different shape.
- Unhandled exceptions become 500 responses; do not leak stack traces or internal messages.

## async def versus def

- `async def` path operations run on the event loop. Any blocking call inside them (synchronous database drivers, `requests`, `time.sleep`, heavy CPU work) blocks every other request handled by that worker.
- Plain `def` path operations and dependencies run in a thread pool, so blocking I/O there does not block the loop. The pool has a limited size (AnyIO's default capacity is 40 threads), so many slow blocking calls still queue.
- Mixing works: call blocking code from `async def` with `await run_in_threadpool(fn, ...)` (Starlette) or `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`.
- CPU-bound work (large DSA computations, model inference) should run in a process pool or a separate worker service; threads do not run Python bytecode in parallel on standard CPython builds.

## Background tasks

`BackgroundTasks` runs small functions after the response is sent, in the same process. It is not a job queue: work is lost if the process restarts, and long tasks occupy the worker. Use a task queue (Celery, RQ, arq, Dramatiq) for durable or long work.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Does this `async def` endpoint call anything that blocks?
- Which fields of your database object would appear in the response without a response model?
- What does the client receive when the request body is missing a required field?

Flask application factory, contexts and Blueprints

This is a framework reference, not DSA-in-Flask context.

## Application factory

```python
def create_app(config: dict | None = None) -> Flask:
    app = Flask(__name__, instance_relative_config=True)
    app.config.from_mapping(SECRET_KEY="dev")
    app.config.from_prefixed_env()          # FLASK_SECRET_KEY, FLASK_DATABASE_URL ...
    if config:
        app.config.update(config)
    db.init_app(app)
    app.register_blueprint(problems_bp, url_prefix="/problems")
    return app
```

Creating the app inside a function lets tests create apps with different configuration and avoids circular imports, because extensions are created at module level without an app and bound later with `init_app`. `flask --app myapp run` finds a `create_app` function automatically.

## Configuration

`app.config` is a dict. Sources include `from_mapping`, `from_object`, `from_pyfile` (often in the instance folder, which is kept out of version control) and `from_prefixed_env` (Flask 2.1+, reads `FLASK_`-prefixed environment variables and parses JSON values). `SECRET_KEY` signs the session cookie; it must be random and secret in production. Debug mode (`--debug`) enables the interactive debugger, which allows code execution and must never be exposed publicly.

## Contexts

Flask uses context-local proxies so that code can access the current app and request without passing them around:

- Application context: `current_app` and `g`. `g` is storage for the duration of one application context (usually one request), commonly used to hold a database connection. It is not shared between requests.
- Request context: `request` and `session`.

Both are pushed automatically while handling a request and in CLI commands. Outside them, such as in a background thread, a script or test setup, accessing `current_app` raises "Working outside of application context". Push one explicitly with `with app.app_context():` (and `app.test_request_context()` for request-dependent code). Context locals are per thread or per async task, so passing the `request` object to another thread does not carry the context with it.

## Teardown

`@app.teardown_appcontext` functions run when the application context ends, even after an exception; they are the place to close per-request resources stored on `g`.

## Blueprints

A `Blueprint` groups routes, templates, static files and error handlers for one part of the application. Register it on the app with an optional `url_prefix`. Endpoint names become `"blueprint_name.view_name"`, so `url_for("problems.detail", pid=3)` builds the URL. Blueprints are registered when the app is created; routes added to a blueprint after registration are not picked up.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Where does this code run, and is an application context active there?
- How would a test create an app with a different database URL?
- What endpoint name does `url_for` need for a view inside this blueprint?

document:
Flask sessions, templates, errors and databases

## Sessions

Flask's default `session` is stored in a cookie signed with `SECRET_KEY`. Signing prevents tampering but does not encrypt: users can read the contents. Do not put secrets in it, keep it small (browsers limit cookie size to about 4 KB), and remember that changing `SECRET_KEY` invalidates all sessions. Server-side sessions need an extension such as Flask-Session. Set `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`, `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY` (true by default) and `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` for production. Mutating a nested object inside the session may need `session.modified = True` so Flask saves it.

Flask has no built-in CSRF protection; form-handling apps typically use Flask-WTF's `CSRFProtect`.

## Templates and escaping

`render_template` uses Jinja. Autoescaping is enabled for templates ending in `.html`, `.htm`, `.xml`, `.xhtml` and, in recent Flask versions, `.svg`, so `{{ value }}` is HTML-escaped there. Strings rendered with `render_template_string`, or templates with other extensions, may not be escaped. `|safe` and `Markup` disable escaping; use them only for trusted, sanitized HTML. Escaping protects HTML text and attribute contexts; it does not make a value safe inside a `<script>` block or a `javascript:` URL.

## Error handling

- `abort(404)` raises an HTTP exception that becomes a response.
- `@app.errorhandler(404)` or `@app.errorhandler(MyError)` customizes responses; blueprints can register their own handlers.
- For JSON APIs, return JSON from handlers (`return {"error": "not found"}, 404`) so clients do not receive HTML error pages.
- Unhandled exceptions become 500 responses in production and the interactive debugger in debug mode. Log them with `app.logger` or a configured logging handler.

## Database integration

Flask has no ORM. Two common patterns:

- The tutorial pattern: open a connection lazily in a helper that stores it on `g`, and close it in a `teardown_appcontext` function. Parameterize queries (`db.execute("... WHERE id = ?", (pid,))`); never format user input into SQL.
- Flask-SQLAlchemy: `db = SQLAlchemy()` at module level, `db.init_app(app)` in the factory. It provides a scoped session tied to the application context (`db.session`) that is removed at the end of each request. Version 3.x requires an active app context for database operations and recommends SQLAlchemy 2.x-style queries (`db.session.execute(db.select(...))`). Use Flask-Migrate (Alembic) for schema migrations.

The N+1 query problem and transaction rules described for other ORMs apply equally: preload relationships the template needs (`selectinload`, `joinedload`), and commit or roll back explicitly.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Who can read the data you stored in this session cookie?
- Is this template rendered with autoescaping on, given its file name and how it is rendered?
- Where is this database connection closed if the view raises?

MicroPython and CircuitPython runtimes

Both are implementations of a Python 3 subset for microcontrollers. CircuitPython is a fork of MicroPython maintained by Adafruit. Code written for one usually does not run unchanged on the other. Every hardware claim should name the runtime, its version, the port (for example rp2, esp32, stm32, nrf) and the board.

## Key differences

| | MicroPython | CircuitPython |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware API | `machine` module: `Pin`, `PWM`, `ADC`, `I2C`, `SPI`, `UART`, `Timer` | `board` (pin names), `digitalio`, `analogio`, `pwmio`, `busio`, plus many native modules |
| Workflow | Files via REPL tools (`mpremote`, Thonny) | Board appears as a USB drive; saving `code.py` restarts it |
| Interrupts | Hardware IRQ callbacks (`Pin.irq`, `Timer`) | No user hardware interrupt callbacks; use `countio`, `keypad` and `asyncio` instead |
| Threads | `_thread` on some ports | Not supported |
| Libraries | `micropython-lib`, `mip` installer | Adafruit library bundle, `circup` |

Both support a subset of `asyncio` for cooperative concurrency.

## Language subset

Not all CPython features or standard library modules exist; many modules are reduced versions (`time`, `os`, `json`, `re`). Check the runtime's "differences from CPython" documentation before assuming a feature. Integers are arbitrary precision on most ports but small integers are stored more cheaply; floating point may be single precision on some ports.

## Memory and garbage collection

RAM is often tens to hundreds of kilobytes. Allocation fails with `MemoryError`, which can happen because of fragmentation even when enough total memory is free.

- Preallocate buffers (`bytearray`, `array`) and reuse them; avoid building strings or lists in tight loops.
- `gc.collect()` at predictable points, and `gc.mem_free()` to observe usage.
- MicroPython offers `micropython.const()` and frozen bytecode (modules compiled into firmware) to save RAM; `.mpy` precompiled files reduce compile-time memory.

## Interrupts (MicroPython)

Interrupt handlers run with constraints documented in "Writing interrupt handlers": a hard IRQ handler must not allocate memory (no creating lists, floats on some ports, or string formatting), must be short, and should share data through preallocated buffers or flags. `micropython.schedule()` defers heavier work to the main context; `micropython.alloc_emergency_exception_buf()` allows exceptions in handlers to be reported. Shared variables updated in an ISR can be read in an inconsistent state unless access is protected (for example by briefly disabling IRQs).

## Timing

Interpreted Python adds overhead per operation; precise timing at microsecond scale is unreliable from Python code. Use hardware peripherals (PWM, timers, PIO on RP2040/RP2350, `rp2` state machines) for precise signals. `time.ticks_ms()`/`ticks_us()` with `ticks_diff()` handle wraparound in MicroPython; CircuitPython uses `time.monotonic_ns()` or `supervisor.ticks_ms()`.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which runtime, version, port and board is this code written for?
- Does anything inside this interrupt handler allocate memory?
- At what point in the loop could memory fragmentation cause a `MemoryError`?

document:
Raspberry Pi GPIO with gpiozero

A Raspberry Pi runs a full Linux operating system with CPython. This is different from microcontroller Python (see the MicroPython/CircuitPython reference): the program shares the CPU with the OS, so timing is not deterministic.

## gpiozero basics

gpiozero offers device classes (`LED`, `Button`, `PWMLED`, `Servo`, `DistanceSensor`, `MotionSensor`) on top of a pin factory backend. On the Raspberry Pi 5, the older RPi.GPIO library does not work because GPIO moved to the RP1 chip; gpiozero uses the lgpio backend there. Check which pin factory is active when behaviour differs between boards (`GPIOZERO_PIN_FACTORY` environment variable).

## Pin numbering

gpiozero uses Broadcom (BCM) GPIO numbers by default: `LED(17)` is GPIO17, which is physical pin 11 on the 40-pin header. Physical numbering is available as `"BOARD11"`, and `"GPIO17"` is also accepted. Mixing numbering schemes is the most common wiring mistake; `pinout` on the command line prints the header layout for the current board.

## Electrical limits (state these, do not guess)

- GPIO pins use 3.3 V logic and are not 5 V tolerant. Connecting a 5 V signal directly can damage the SoC; use a level shifter or a voltage divider.
- Each GPIO pin can source or sink only a small current. Drive LEDs through a resistor and drive motors, relays and solenoids through a transistor or driver board, with a flyback diode for inductive loads.
- Always connect grounds between the Pi and external circuits.

Exact current ratings and power budgets depend on the board model and are given in the Raspberry Pi documentation and datasheets; quote them from there rather than from memory.

## Inputs

`Button(pin, pull_up=True)` enables an internal pull-up, so the input reads high until the button connects it to ground. Floating inputs read random values. Mechanical switches bounce; `bounce_time` filters it in software. Callbacks such as `when_pressed` run in a background thread, so shared state needs the usual thread-safety care.

## Buses

I2C, SPI and UART must be enabled (for example with `raspi-config` or `config.txt` overlays) before use. Use libraries such as `smbus2` or `spidev`, or the device driver's Python package. On many models the primary UART is used by the serial console or Bluetooth by default; follow the board-specific UART configuration documentation.

## Failure assumptions to state explicitly

- Wiring and pin numbers match the diagram for the stated board model.
- I2C devices respond at the expected address (`i2cdetect -y 1` lists them); a missing device raises `OSError` on access.
- Sensor reads can fail or return stale values; code should handle timeouts and retries.
- Running as a user in the `gpio` (and `i2c`, `spi`) groups is needed for access without root.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which numbering scheme does the number in your code use, and which physical pin is it?
- What voltage does this sensor output, and what does the Pi's input pin accept?
- What happens in your code if the I2C device is unplugged?

Embedded C startup, linker scripts and provenance

## What happens before main

On a bare-metal microcontroller there is no operating system to load the program. After reset (for Arm Cortex-M):

1. The core reads the initial stack pointer and the reset handler address from the vector table at the start of flash (or the configured vector table address).
2. The reset handler, usually in a vendor or CMSIS startup file, may call `SystemInit` to configure clocks and flash wait states.
3. It copies initialized data (`.data`) from flash to RAM and zeroes `.bss`. This is what makes C's rules for static storage (initialized values, zero by default) true on the device.
4. It may run C++ constructors and C library initialization, then calls `main`.

If `main` returns, behaviour depends on the startup code; most firmware never returns from `main`.

## Sections and the linker script

The linker script (for GNU ld, a `.ld` file) defines memory regions (`FLASH`, `RAM`, sometimes `CCMRAM`, `ITCM`, `DTCM`) and places sections into them:

- `.isr_vector` (vector table), `.text` (code), `.rodata` (constants) in flash.
- `.data` with a load address in flash and a run address in RAM.
- `.bss`, heap and stack in RAM.

Symbols defined in the script (`_sdata`, `_edata`, `_sbss`, `_estack`, names vary) are used by the startup code. A mismatch between the script and the actual device memory (wrong size or origin) leads to hard faults or silently corrupted data. Use the linker script that matches the exact part number.

`__attribute__((section(".name")))` places objects in custom sections, for example a buffer in DMA-capable RAM. The map file (`-Wl,-Map=out.map`) shows where everything ended up and how much memory is used.

## Stack and heap

Stack size is fixed by the linker script or startup file. Stack overflow on a bare-metal device usually corrupts adjacent memory rather than producing an error. Measure stack use (`-fstack-usage`, stack painting) and avoid deep recursion and large local arrays; DSA code ported to MCUs often needs iterative versions and static buffers. Many embedded coding standards restrict or forbid dynamic allocation after initialization.

## Hard faults

Typical causes: invalid memory access, unaligned access where not supported, executing from a bad address, stack overflow, divide by zero when trapping is enabled. Cortex-M fault status registers (CFSR, HFSR, MMFAR, BFAR) and the stacked program counter identify the faulting instruction.

## Provenance checklist for embedded examples

The existing embedded C material lacks this context. For each example or claim, record:

- MCU part number, core and silicon revision when errata matter.
- Board and its wiring (pins, pull-ups, external parts).
- Toolchain, version and flags; C standard.
- Vendor SDK/HAL or register headers and version; RTOS and version if any.
- Clock tree settings (oscillator, PLL, bus prescalers), which determine timer and baud rate calculations.
- Electrical limits relied on (voltage levels, current, timing), cited from the datasheet.
- Whether the code was built and run on hardware, and how.

Claims without these should be presented as illustrative, not device-verified.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Where in memory does this array end up, according to the map file?
- Which code copies `.data` into RAM, and what happens to a global that is read before that?
- Which clock frequency is your timer calculation assuming, and where is it configured?

document:
Embedded C: volatile, atomics and interrupts

## What volatile does

`volatile` tells the compiler that every access to the object is a side effect: it must not cache the value in a register, remove reads or writes, or merge them. It is required for:

- Memory-mapped peripheral registers (normally declared through vendor or CMSIS headers).
- Variables written by an interrupt service routine (ISR) and read in the main loop, so the loop sees updates.

## What volatile does not do

- It does not make an operation atomic. `counter++` on a `volatile uint32_t` is still read, modify, write; an ISR that fires in between loses an update.
- It does not make multi-byte reads consistent. On an 8-bit MCU, reading a 16-bit or 32-bit variable takes several instructions; an ISR can change it halfway.
- It does not order accesses to non-volatile variables, and it is not a memory barrier between CPU cores or for DMA.

## Protecting shared data

Choose based on the target:

- Disable interrupts briefly around the access (`__disable_irq()`/`__enable_irq()` in CMSIS, or save and restore PRIMASK so nesting is safe). Keep the critical section short to protect interrupt latency.
- Use C11 `<stdatomic.h>` where the compiler and target support lock-free atomics for that size. On Cortex-M3 and later, word-sized atomics are typically implemented with exclusive load/store instructions; on Cortex-M0/M0+ they may require library support or interrupt masking.
- Single-producer, single-consumer ring buffers with one index written only by the ISR and the other only by the main loop avoid locks when each index update is atomic on the target.

## ISR rules

- Keep ISRs short: capture data, clear the interrupt flag, signal the main loop.
- Clear the peripheral's interrupt flag as documented; failing to clear it can re-enter the ISR immediately. On some MCUs the clear takes effect a few cycles later, and vendor notes recommend a read-back or barrier before returning.
- Do not call non-reentrant functions (`malloc`, most of `stdio`) from an ISR.
- Priorities and nesting are configured in the interrupt controller (NVIC on Cortex-M). With an RTOS, only call API functions marked as ISR-safe (for example the `FromISR` variants in FreeRTOS), and respect the RTOS's maximum syscall interrupt priority.

## DMA and caches

On MCUs with data caches (for example Cortex-M7), a buffer written by DMA may not be visible to the CPU until the cache is invalidated, and CPU writes must be cleaned to memory before DMA reads them. Buffers need alignment to the cache line size. `volatile` does not solve this. Follow the MCU reference manual.

## Provenance to record

Every embedded example should state: MCU part number and core, board, toolchain and version (GCC Arm, Clang, IAR, Keil), optimization level, vendor HAL or register headers and version, clock configuration, and how pins are wired. Without these, register names, timing and interrupt behaviour cannot be verified.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- If the interrupt fires between the read and the write of this counter, what value is stored?
- How many instructions does reading this variable take on your MCU?
- Which interrupt flag does this ISR clear, and when?

HTML versus DOM, JavaScript and Web APIs

Retrieval works better when each topic has one owner. Use this map to decide which reference (and which language subject) a question belongs to.

| Question about | Owned by | Reference subject |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Elements, attributes, parsing, forms, `<dialog>`, `<template>`, browsing contexts, history, the event loop | HTML Living Standard | html |
| Nodes, `Element`, `querySelector`, events and `addEventListener`, `MutationObserver`, `AbortSignal` | DOM Living Standard | html (with javascript cross-link) |
| Syntax, types, closures, promises, modules | ECMAScript | javascript |
| Layout, selectors, cascade, animation | CSS specifications | css |
| `fetch`, Storage, IndexedDB, Web Workers, Geolocation, Clipboard, WebSocket, Canvas | Separate API specifications (WHATWG and W3C) | javascript (Web API section) |

## Lifecycle

- Parsing and `DOMContentLoaded`: the DOM is built; deferred scripts (`<script defer>`, module scripts) have run. `load` fires after subresources such as images finish.
- `async` scripts run as soon as they download, in any order; `defer` scripts run in document order after parsing; classic scripts without either block parsing.
- `visibilitychange` (with `document.visibilityState`) signals that the page was hidden; it is the reliable last chance to save state, especially on mobile. `beforeunload` and `unload` are unreliable, and `unload` is being deprecated.
- The back/forward cache can restore a page without reloading it; `pageshow` with `event.persisted` detects that.

## Permissions

Powerful features (camera, microphone, geolocation, notifications, clipboard read) require user permission, a secure context (HTTPS or localhost), and often a user gesture. `navigator.permissions.query()` reports state for some permissions. Permissions Policy (`allow` attribute on `<iframe>`, `Permissions-Policy` header) controls which frames may request them.

## Security boundaries

- Same-origin policy: scripts can read responses and DOM only from the same scheme, host and port, unless the other origin allows it through CORS. CORS is enforced by the browser on reading responses; it does not stop the request from being sent.
- Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts where scripts, styles and other resources may load from and can block inline scripts, limiting cross-site scripting.
- `<iframe sandbox>` removes capabilities from embedded content; `rel="noopener"` (the default for `target="_blank"` links in current browsers) prevents the opened page from controlling the opener.
- Cookies: `HttpOnly` hides them from scripts, `Secure` limits them to HTTPS, `SameSite` controls cross-site sending.
- Inserting untrusted strings with `innerHTML` executes markup; `textContent` does not. The Trusted Types API and sanitizers help enforce this.

## Linking topics

When a reference record mixes these concerns, tag it with the owning standard and cross-link the others instead of duplicating content. This keeps learner answers from attributing, for example, `fetch` behaviour to HTML or form validation to JavaScript.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which specification defines the API you are asking about?
- When does this script run relative to parsing, given how it is included?
- Which origin served this response, and which origin is trying to read it?

CSS cascade, layers and specificity

The existing CSS records list properties. This reference explains how the browser decides which declaration wins and what value is finally used.

## Cascade order

When several declarations set the same property on the same element, the cascade sorts them by these criteria, in order; the first that differs decides:

1. Origin and importance: user-agent, user and author styles, with `!important` declarations reversing the order of origins. Transitions and animations have their own positions.
2. Context (shadow DOM encapsulation).
3. Element-attached styles (the `style` attribute).
4. Cascade layers.
5. Specificity.
6. Order of appearance: later wins.

## Cascade layers

`@layer reset, base, components, utilities;` declares layer order. For normal declarations, later layers win over earlier ones regardless of specificity, and unlayered styles win over all layers. For `!important` declarations the layer order is reversed. Layers let frameworks and resets have low priority without specificity tricks. Tailwind CSS v4 and some other tools emit layered CSS, which changes how custom styles interact with them.

## Specificity

Specificity is compared as three numbers (A, B, C): A counts ID selectors, B counts classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, C counts type selectors and pseudo-elements. Universal selector and combinators add nothing.

- `:is()`, `:not()` and `:has()` take the specificity of their most specific argument; `:where()` always has zero specificity.
- Inline `style` attributes beat any selector (step 3 above), except `!important` declarations from stylesheets.
- Raising specificity to win (chaining classes, adding IDs) makes later overrides harder; layers and low-specificity selectors scale better.

## Inheritance

Some properties inherit by default (`color`, `font-*`, `line-height`, `visibility`, `cursor`), most do not (`margin`, `border`, `background`, `width`, `display`). The keywords `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert` and `revert-layer` control this explicitly. `revert` rolls back to the previous origin (often the browser default); `revert-layer` to the previous layer.

## Value stages

- Specified value: the result of the cascade, inheritance, or the initial value.
- Computed value: relative values resolved as far as possible without layout (for example `em` to `px` for `font-size`, `currentColor` kept as a keyword). This is what inherits.
- Used value: after layout, such as percentages of a container's width turned into pixels.
- Actual value: after device constraints such as rounding.

`getComputedStyle()` returns resolved values, which are computed values for some properties and used values for others (for example `width` of a rendered element). Explanations of "why is my width X" usually need the used value, which depends on layout.

## Debugging

Browser dev tools show matched rules in cascade order with overridden declarations crossed out, the layer each rule belongs to, and the computed panel shows final values with their origin.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which cascade step decides between these two rules: layer, specificity or order?
- Is this property inherited, or does the child get its initial value?
- Are you looking at the computed value or the used value?

Sass: modules, configuration and compilation

Sass is a stylesheet language compiled to CSS. SCSS syntax (`.scss`) is a superset of CSS; the indented syntax (`.sass`) omits braces and semicolons. This record is separate from plain CSS and from Bootstrap, which uses Sass internally.

## Implementations

Dart Sass (npm package `sass`, or `sass-embedded`) is the maintained implementation. LibSass and node-sass are deprecated and do not support the module system. Version-sensitive answers should name the Dart Sass version.

## The module system

- `@use "tokens";` loads a module once per compilation and namespaces its members: `tokens.$primary`, `tokens.spacing(2)`. `@use "tokens" as t;` renames the namespace; `as *` removes it.
- Members whose names start with `-` or `_` are private to their module.
- `@forward "tokens";` re-exports a module's members from another file, which is how libraries build a single entry point. `show`/`hide` limit what is forwarded.
- Partials (`_tokens.scss`) are not compiled on their own; `@use "tokens"` finds them.

## Configuration

`@use "library" with ($primary: #0055aa);` sets variables declared with `!default` in that module. A module can be configured only the first time it is loaded in a compilation. Because of this, configure libraries in one place.

## Deprecated @import

`@import` makes every variable, mixin and function global, may load the same file several times, and gives no namespaces. It is deprecated (warnings since Dart Sass 1.80) and planned for removal in Dart Sass 3.0. The `sass-migrator` tool converts many projects to `@use`. Global built-in functions such as `darken()` and `map-get()` are also being deprecated in favour of module functions (`color.adjust`, `color.scale`, `map.get` from `sass:color`, `sass:map`).

## Functions and mixins

- `@function` returns a value with `@return`; use for calculations.
- `@mixin` emits declarations or rules; include with `@include`. Mixins accept arguments with defaults and a `@content` block.
- Built-in modules: `sass:math` (`math.div` replaces `/` for division, which is ambiguous with CSS slash syntax), `sass:color`, `sass:list`, `sass:map`, `sass:string`, `sass:meta`, `sass:selector`.
- Control flow: `@if`, `@each`, `@for`, `@while` run at compile time.

## Compilation

`sass src/main.scss dist/main.css --style=compressed --source-map` compiles from the command line; build tools (Vite, webpack's sass-loader) call the same compiler. Errors and deprecation warnings appear at build time, not in the browser. `--quiet-deps` silences warnings from dependencies but not from your own code. Sass variables are compile-time; CSS custom properties (`--primary`) are run-time and can change with media queries or JavaScript.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Is this variable available in this file through `@use`, or only because of a global `@import`?
- Which file configures this library, and is it the first to load it?
- Does this value need to change at run time? Should it be a Sass variable or a custom property?

Bootstrap 5

Bootstrap is a CSS and JavaScript component framework. This record is separate from plain CSS and Sass; answers about Bootstrap should name the major and minor version, because class names and behaviour changed between 3, 4 and 5.

## Layout and utilities

- Grid: `.container`, `.row`, `.col-*` with breakpoints `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `xxl`. The grid is built on flexbox; gutters use `g-*` classes.
- Utilities: spacing (`m-3`, `px-2`, using a logical scale), display (`d-none d-md-block`), flex (`d-flex justify-content-between`), text and colour (`text-body-secondary`, `bg-primary`), sizing, borders and position. Version 5 renamed directional utilities to logical start/end (`ms-*`, `me-*` instead of `ml-*`, `mr-*`) to support RTL.
- The Utility API (in Sass) generates utilities from maps, so projects can add, remove or modify utilities at build time.

## Components

Buttons, forms, cards, navbars, modals, dropdowns, tooltips, popovers, toasts, accordions, carousels, offcanvas and more. Each component's documentation lists required markup and ARIA attributes; leaving out the documented attributes breaks keyboard and screen reader support. Components marked as interactive need Bootstrap's JavaScript.

## Customizing: Sass and CSS variables

- Sass: import Bootstrap's source and override `!default` variables (`$primary`, `$enable-shadows`, `$grid-breakpoints`) before Bootstrap's variables load, or modify maps through the documented functions. Bootstrap 5.3's Sass sources still use `@import` internally, so compiling them with recent Dart Sass prints deprecation warnings; see the Sass reference. Check the Bootstrap release notes for its plan.
- CSS variables: compiled CSS exposes tokens such as `--bs-primary`, `--bs-body-bg` and component-level variables (`--bs-btn-padding-x`). Changing them at run time adjusts appearance without recompiling.
- Color modes (5.3+): `data-bs-theme="dark"` on an element switches its subtree to the dark palette.

## JavaScript

Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery. Its plugins are ES modules bundled as `bootstrap.bundle.js` (which includes Popper for dropdowns, tooltips and popovers) or imported individually.

- Many components initialize automatically through data attributes (`data-bs-toggle="modal"` with `data-bs-target="#id"`).
- Tooltips and popovers are opt-in for performance: they must be initialized in JavaScript (`new bootstrap.Tooltip(el)`).
- Events such as `show.bs.modal` and `hidden.bs.modal` let code react to component state.
- Content inserted dynamically after initialization may need components to be created for it.

## Common problems

- Mixing class names from different major versions (for example `ml-2` from Bootstrap 4) silently does nothing in 5.
- Dropdowns or tooltips not working usually means Popper is missing (use the bundle) or the plugin was not initialized.
- Overriding styles with higher-specificity selectors instead of variables leads to fragile CSS; prefer variables or Sass configuration.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which Bootstrap version does this project load, and does this class exist in it?
- Does this component need JavaScript, and has it been initialized?
- Could this colour change be made by setting a variable instead of a new selector?

Tailwind CSS

Tailwind generates small single-purpose classes (`flex`, `px-4`, `text-sm`, `bg-sky-500`) from the class names it finds in your source files. This record covers Tailwind only; Bulma and shadcn/ui have separate records.

## Utility syntax

- Utilities map to one or a few declarations: `p-4` is `padding: calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` in v4 (`1rem` with the default spacing).
- Arbitrary values: `w-[37rem]`, `grid-cols-[200px_1fr]` (underscores stand for spaces), `bg-(--brand)` in v4 for a CSS variable (v3 used `bg-[--brand]` or `bg-[var(--brand)]`).
- Important modifier: `bg-red-500!` in v4 (trailing), `!bg-red-500` in v3.

## Variants

Prefixes apply a utility conditionally: `hover:`, `focus-visible:`, `disabled:`, `aria-expanded:`, `data-[state=open]:`, `group-hover:`, `peer-checked:`, `dark:`, `motion-reduce:`, responsive `sm:`, `md:`, `lg:` (mobile-first min-width breakpoints), and container queries `@container` with `@md:` (built in since v4). Variants stack: `md:hover:underline`. In v4, stacked variants apply left to right, which changed compared with v3 for some combinations.

## Configuration in v4

v4 is configured in CSS:

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
@theme {
  --color-brand: oklch(0.6 0.2 250);
  --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem;
}
```

Theme variables in `@theme` create utilities (`bg-brand`) and are also emitted as CSS custom properties. `@utility` defines custom utilities, `@variant`/`@custom-variant` define variants, `@plugin` loads plugins, and `@config` can still load a legacy `tailwind.config.js`. In v3, configuration lived in `tailwind.config.js` and CSS used `@tailwind base; @tailwind components; @tailwind utilities;`.

## Source detection

v4 scans the project automatically, skipping files ignored by `.gitignore`, binary files and CSS files. `@source "../node_modules/some-lib";` adds paths; `@source not` excludes them. In v3, the `content` array in the config listed files explicitly.

Because classes are found by scanning text, class names must appear whole in source code. Building them from pieces (`"bg-" + color + "-500"`) produces classes Tailwind never sees, so no CSS is generated. Map values to complete class names instead.

## Cascade layers

v4 output uses native CSS cascade layers (`theme`, `base`, `components`, `utilities`). Unlayered custom CSS beats all layered Tailwind utilities regardless of specificity; see the CSS cascade reference. This explains many "my utility doesn't apply" reports after migrating.

## Migrating from v3 to v4

The official upgrade tool (`npx @tailwindcss/upgrade`) automates much of the migration. Notable changes: new CSS-first configuration; some utilities renamed (`shadow-sm` → `shadow-xs`, `rounded-sm` → `rounded-xs`, `outline-none` → `outline-hidden`, and others), and the bare names moved up one step (`shadow` → `shadow-sm`, `rounded` → `rounded-sm`, `blur` → `blur-sm`), so an unchanged `shadow-sm` silently gets smaller; default border colour changed to `currentColor`; ring width default changed from 3px to 1px (replace `ring` with `ring-3` to keep the old look); PostCSS plugin moved to `@tailwindcss/postcss`, with a dedicated `@tailwindcss/vite` plugin, and the CLI moved to `@tailwindcss/cli`; modern browser baseline (Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+, Firefox 128+). Check the upgrade guide for the full list.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Does the complete class name appear anywhere in your source files?
- Which Tailwind major version is installed, and which syntax is this config written in?
- Is there unlayered CSS overriding this utility?

Bulma

Bulma is a CSS framework of components and helpers built on flexbox. This record separates it from Tailwind, with which it previously shared a source.

## CSS only

Bulma ships no JavaScript. Components that need behaviour (a navbar burger that toggles a menu, a dropdown that opens on click, a modal that opens and closes) only provide the styles and the `is-active` state class. Your own code must toggle the class and handle keyboard and focus behaviour, including ARIA attributes such as `aria-expanded` and focus management for modals. Answers that describe Bulma components "opening" must say which script does it.

This differs from Bootstrap, which includes JavaScript plugins, and from Tailwind, which provides utilities rather than components.

## Class conventions

- Components and elements: `button`, `card`, `navbar`, `modal`, `tabs`, `notification`, `columns`/`column`.
- Modifiers with `is-` or `has-` prefixes: `is-primary`, `is-large`, `is-loading`, `is-active`, `has-text-centered`.
- Columns: `columns` container with `column` children; sizes such as `is-half` or `is-4` (12-column scale), and responsive modifiers such as `is-half-tablet`. Breakpoints are named `mobile`, `tablet`, `desktop`, `widescreen`, `fullhd`.
- Helpers for spacing (`m-2`, `px-4`), typography, colours, flexbox and visibility (`is-hidden-mobile`).

## Theming in Bulma 1.0

Bulma 1.0 rewrote the framework around CSS custom properties (prefixed `--bulma-`) and the Dart Sass module system:

- Run-time theming by setting variables such as `--bulma-primary-h` (hue), `--bulma-primary-s` and `--bulma-primary-l`, since colours are defined in HSL parts.
- Built-in light and dark themes that follow `prefers-color-scheme`, overridable with `data-theme` or theme classes.
- Sass customization with `@use "bulma/sass" with ($primary: ...)`. Bulma 0.9.x used `@import` and Sass-only variables; code written for 0.9 may need changes.

## Accessibility notes

Because there is no JavaScript, accessibility of interactive patterns depends entirely on the project's code. Use native elements where possible (`<button>` for the burger), and follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices for menus, tabs and dialogs.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Which part of your code adds `is-active` to this menu, and what does it do for keyboard users?
- Is this project on Bulma 0.9 or 1.0, and how does that change how you set the primary colour?
- Which breakpoint name corresponds to the screen width you are testing?

shadcn/ui

shadcn/ui is not a component library installed as a package. Its CLI copies component source files into your project (typically `components/ui/`), and from then on you own and maintain that code. This record separates it from Tailwind and Bulma.

## What gets copied, and what it depends on

- React components written in TypeScript, styled with Tailwind utility classes.
- Behaviour and accessibility from headless primitives, mainly Radix UI (dialogs, dropdown menus, popovers, tabs, tooltips), plus libraries for specific components (for example a date picker or a command menu).
- Helpers such as `cn()` (combining `clsx` and `tailwind-merge`) and `class-variance-authority` for variants.
- `components.json` records the project's style, aliases, Tailwind configuration and base colour, and tells the CLI where to write files.

`npx shadcn@latest add dialog` adds the component and installs its npm dependencies. Updating means re-running the CLI or diffing against the upstream source; there is no `npm update` for copied files. Local edits make updates a manual merge.

## State and accessibility contracts

The Radix primitives handle focus management, keyboard interaction and ARIA attributes for their patterns (a `Dialog` traps focus and restores it on close; a `DropdownMenu` supports arrow-key navigation). Those guarantees hold only while the component structure the primitive expects is kept: for example `DialogTitle` must remain (Radix warns when a dialog has no accessible title), triggers should stay buttons or use `asChild` correctly, and controlled state (`open`/`onOpenChange`) must be wired consistently. Removing or replacing parts while restyling can silently break accessibility.

State is regular React state: components accept controlled (`open` plus `onOpenChange`) or uncontrolled (`defaultOpen`) usage, following Radix's API.

## Theming

Colours are CSS variables (`--background`, `--foreground`, `--primary`, ...) defined in the global stylesheet and mapped to Tailwind theme colours. Dark mode switches the variable values, usually with a `.dark` class. With Tailwind v4, variables are mapped through `@theme inline` and colour values default to OKLCH in recent templates; Tailwind v3 projects map them in `tailwind.config.js` with HSL values. Mixing instructions for the two setups is a common source of broken themes.

## Integration notes

- Framework support: Next.js, Vite, React Router, Astro, Laravel and others, each with an installation guide. Server and client component boundaries matter in Next.js; interactive components are marked `"use client"`.
- Because the code lives in your repository, lint, test and review it like your own code.

## Mentor prompts (no answers)
- Is this component's file in your repository, or imported from a package? Who updates it?
- Did the restyled dialog keep the parts Radix needs for focus and labelling?
- Which Tailwind version does this project's `components.json` and stylesheet assume?
